discovery: Development of silicon microstrip and hybrid/3D pixel detectors for precision vertexing and particle imaging

nominees.name: Erik H. M. Heijne
nominees.affiliation: CERN (emeritus); Institute of Experimental and Applied Physics, Czech Technical University in Prague

motivation: Heijne pioneered planar silicon microstrip detectors for high-energy physics (CERN NA11/NA32, early 1980s), first resolving charm-particle decay vertices at micron precision, and then led the development of hybrid pixel detectors with bump-bonded readout chips. Parker invented 3D silicon sensors and helped originate monolithic active pixels, giving radiation-hard, fast, finely segmented sensors. Campbell developed the Medipix/Timepix family of photon-counting and timing pixel chips, carrying pixel technology into X-ray imaging, medicine and space dosimetry. Silicon vertex trackers based on this work made b-quark identification routine. That capability was essential to the discovery of the top quark and to establishing the Higgs boson's couplings to heavy fermions. Today every collider experiment and many imaging instruments rely on these detectors. Their work turned silicon into precise instruments for measuring particle trajectories and made new measurements possible.
